passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with mildly elevated blood pressure. One hundred twenty participants were randomly assigned to receive either the drug (n = 60) or a placebo (n = 60) for eight weeks. Baseline SBP was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest. After the treatment period, SBP was reassessed. The study aimed to determine whether the drug lowered SBP more effectively than placebo and to assess the magnitude of change. The investigators also collected data on adverse events and adherence. The results were summarized in Table 1 below, which lists mean SBP and standard deviation (SD) at baseline, after eight weeks, and the mean change for each group.
stem: Which group experienced the greater reduction in systolic blood pressure after 8 weeks?

options.C: Both groups experienced the same reduction

explanation: The drug group’s mean SBP decreased from 120 mmHg to 110 mmHg, a 10 mmHg drop, whereas the placebo group’s mean SBP decreased only 1 mmHg. Therefore, the drug group had the greater reduction.
trap: Concluding both groups reduced equally because both fell; the drug group fell 10 mmHg and the placebo group 1 mmHg.

stem: What type of study design was employed in this research?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to the drug or placebo group, and the effect was measured over time, which defines a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Choosing a cohort design because participants were followed; random assignment defines an RCT.

stem: Calculate the percent reduction in systolic blood pressure for the drug group.
explanation: Percent reduction = [(120 – 110)/120] × 100 = 8.33 %. The other options are incorrect calculations.
trap: Mis-dividing or reporting the absolute change; (120 − 110)/120 × 100 = 8.33%, not 10%.

stem: Which feature of this trial best reduces selection bias?

options.A: Random assignment to drug or placebo
options.B: Measuring SBP after a 5-minute seated rest

explanation: Random assignment gives each participant the same chance of receiving either treatment, which balances known and unknown characteristics. Seated rest standardizes measurement; duration and safety data do not affect selection.
trap: Choosing seated rest: it reduces measurement variability, not selection bias.

stem: Which statement is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The drug group’s mean SBP fell by about 9 mmHg more than the placebo group’s mean SBP.
options.B: The placebo group’s mean SBP rose over the eight weeks.
options.C: The two groups differed at baseline by more than 10 mmHg.
options.D: The mean 8-week SBP of the drug group was only 1 mmHg lower than that of the placebo group.

explanation: Correct: A) Mean change was -10 mmHg with the drug and -1 mmHg with placebo, a difference of 9 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: B) Placebo SBP fell from 119 to 118 mmHg, so it did not rise. C) Baselines were 120 and 119 mmHg, a 1 mmHg difference. D) 8-week means were 110 and 118 mmHg, an 8 mmHg difference.
trap: Reading the placebo group’s 1 mmHg change as no change at all, or misreading the 8-week means as nearly equal.
